items.title: Part 3: Knowing when your agent doesn’t know: the confidence layer
items.summary: Trustworthy production LLM systems must engineer confidence from verifiable independent signals, calibrate it against actual accuracy, and treat human handoffs as a self-improving feedback loop rather than a rubber-stamp.
ideas: Compose confidence from independent signals; weight model self-report lowest since it cannot be independently verified
Calibrate composed scores with isotonic regression so '0.9' actually means 90% correctness
ECE is binning-sensitive and can mask miscalibration; prefer Brier score or signed per-bucket gaps for alerting
Abstention is a first-class outcome and the best defense against unknown unknowns in production
Adversarial judge prompts asking 'why is this wrong' catch far more failures than agreeable reviewers
Sample the judge: 100% on high-stakes, always on borderline, 5-10% random as a quality probe
Judge disagreement rate is a health signal; spikes indicate attacks, bad deploys, or model regressions
Use deterministic hashes instead of RNG for sampling so agent behavior stays testable and reproducible
Approve/reject handoffs manufacture false accountability; show editable drafts with reasoning and evidence instead
Human edits are the richest training signal; corrected answers become golden-set evaluation cases
Unanimous human approvals justify lowering thresholds; frequent overrides pull slices back to human-only
Calibration rots; a quarter-old threshold is a quarter-old risk model and needs rolling recomputation
A single global threshold fails because different slices have wildly different baseline accuracy

items.title: kTLS Sends the File Without Copying It
items.summary: FreeBSD's kTLS reuses its 23-year sendfile infrastructure to reduce TLS file-serving system calls to 2.1% of the userland equivalent and deliver 4x CPU efficiency gains, outperforming Linux by roughly 2x in matched benchmarks due to vertical integration of the kernel stack.
ideas: kTLS on FreeBSD cuts nginx write calls from 131,080 to 2,746 sendfile calls for 2GB transfers

Same nginx config line yields 29% throughput gain on FreeBSD vs 13% on Ubuntu 21.10
Intel found kTLS sendfile beats userland above ~64KB files, loses below 4KB
Gallatin's 2019 NUMA siloing took a Xeon 4216 from 105 to 191 Gb/s
Netflix measured 731 Gb/s from a dual-socket FreeBSD box with inline NIC crypto
kTLS code path is 2,503 lines in uipc_ktls.c, in GENERIC, on by default since 15.0
Author's Ryzen test showed worker CPU time falling 7.07s to 0.26s for 10GB
items.rating_reason: Exceptional technical depth combining original DTrace measurements, named contributor history dating to 1998, specific implementation details (line counts, mbuf chain ratios, sysctl names), and cross-platform benchmarks from multiple independent sources. The article traces a 23-year chain of FreeBSD kernel features (sendfile, async flag, mbufs, kTLS, RACK/BBR, NUMA siloing, lagg) with reproducible numbers at every step. It also honestly engages with 2026 security advisories as limitations. Truncation at the end is a minor blemish on an otherwise exemplary piece of systems engineering writing.

ideas: SSH forwarding-enabled config persists after reboot; the tunnel itself vanishes, so hunt the setting
forwarding-enabled=no is the default; any other value means someone deliberately enabled pivoting capability
WAN-reachable SSH plus undocumented forwarding changes indicate an outside door, not internal tooling
Enabled SOCKS proxy with auth-method=none and WAN reachability forms an unauthenticated open relay
Web proxy redirect-to pointing externally with non-zero hits proves active client traffic tampering

dst-nat alone doesn't expose internal hosts; audit NAT and forward filter chains together
Attackers camouflage malicious firewall rules with innocent comments like 'bandwidth-monitor' on RDP ports
Disabled firewall rules can be sleeping port forwards activated later via a scheduler
Public domains in DNS static tables resolving to external IPs signal hijacking; internal targets are routine
DNS regexp entries matching public domains enable mass interception beyond a single local override
Scheduler chains link system scripts to on-event triggers, providing toolless attacker persistence
Sensitive ports (3389, 445, 22) exposed with empty src-address accept connections from anywhere

items.title: https://blog.securelayer7.net/cve-2026-73570-zimbra-command-injection/

CORDIC needs only shifts and adds using precomputed arctan(2^-n) special angles

FPTAN returns partial tangent coordinates, making the final division free or deferrable
Pseudo-division selects CORDIC decision bits before any rotations are actually applied
Rotations are applied smallest-angle-first to reduce accumulated rounding error
The 8087 stores all values as 80-bit temporary reals with a 16383 exponent bias
Register stack tags (zero, valid, special, empty) enable overflow and underflow detection
Guard, round, and sticky bits in tmpC support precise rounding during calculations
FPTAN computed tangents in 90 microseconds versus 13,000 on the 8086

items.title: Why model versioning is not enough for production AI
items.summary: A deployed AI system is a combination of model, prompts, retrieval, tools, and runtime settings—true production reliability requires bundling, testing, and replaying that entire release as one unit, not just versioning model weights.
ideas: Model version is only one dependency; prompts, retrieval, tools, and runtime change behavior independently.
A versioned release manifest with resolvable references is the practical starting point, not a bigger platform.
Manifests are not reproducibility promises; record nondeterminism limits and ingestion watermarks honestly.
Sequentially updating four config stores is not an atomic release; resolve the tested combination consistently.
Evaluation gates should test the full path—retrieval through output validation—not just model calls with prepared prompts.
Keep held-out evaluation data so repeated prompt tuning doesn't turn the whole suite into a training target.
Prefer deterministic checks; model-judge scores need pinned configuration and human review of disagreements.
Set acceptance criteria before examining the candidate, and make failed gates emit debugging artifacts.
Load test distributions of input length, output length, concurrency, and bursts, not just requests per second.
Separate time-to-first-token, token pace, and queue time; users spend most latency waiting in queues.
Never sum per-stage percentiles to claim end-to-end p95; they may describe different requests.
Benchmark the batching scheduler you actually run; batching trades user-visible delay for throughput.
GPU utilization is a diagnostic signal, not the product objective—measure user experience instead.
Compute cost per successful task, counting retries and escalations, not cost per request.
A release that looks cheaper because it silently truncates answers should fail evaluation, not win on cost.
Rollback must restore compatible dependencies; routing to old app code can still read a new retrieval index.
Tool side effects like emails or record updates need idempotency and approval boundaries; model rollback cannot undo them.
Historical index snapshots must still honor current access revocations and deletion requirements.
Feed incidents back into versioned evaluation suites, but recognize production feedback is selective and biased.
Assign ownership at interfaces and empower someone to stop a rollout; an alert without an empowered actor is incomplete.
items.rating_reason: This is dense, expert-level MLOps content from a practitioner engineer with numerous genuine value instances: a concrete versioned release manifest covering prompts, retrieval indices, and runtime config; practical evaluation gate design with held-out datasets and deterministic checks; correct statistical advice that per-stage percentiles cannot be summed into end-to-end p95; a cost-per-successful-task accounting method that counts retries; and rollback-as-routing with the subtle failure modes of incompatible index versions, in-flight request draining, and irreversible tool side effects. The content is well-attributed (Google MLOps, vLLM, Triton, SRE Workbook) and efficiently structured with minimal fluff in the article body. Thematic alignment is strong across AI, Tech, and Sysadmin themes. A minor deduction for the surrounding site boilerplate inflating the content envelope and because the piece synthesizes established guidance (Google MLOps, SRE canarying) for generative applications rather than introducing novel research.

items.summary: A single rounding-off-by-one chroma row in libheif becomes full remote code execution by leaking library bases through returned image pixels, forging plane maps into a write-what-where, overwriting memcpy@GOT, and reusing libvips's internal GLib loader instead of a ROP chain.
ideas: Rounding mismatch between destination row and copy height lets a fourth tile write one extra chroma row past allocation
A controlled 58-byte overflow becomes exploitable via forged plane-map entries redirecting Cr-plane copies to attacker-chosen destinations
Uninitialized alpha-channel bytes in returned PNGs expose libvips pointers, defeating ASLR without any direct memory read
Overwriting memcpy@GOT mid-loop hijacks control flow on the very next row, minimizing the window for state disturbance
Reusing libvips's internal g_module_open_full routine wraps dlopen so hijacked control flow loads attacker-supplied shared objects without ROP
Versioned native-stack profiles with verified byte signatures and offsets make exploits portable across Ubuntu and Debian builds
All runtime code addresses derive from the leaked libvips base, so PIE Node executables never need their randomized address recovered
Web routes passing attacker-controlled files into native decoder chains create attack surfaces beyond OWASP Top 10 coverage
Heap selectors derive from measured allocator page-lane relationships, not OS names, requiring per-build calibration
items.rating_reason: This is original vulnerability research with exceptional technical depth: the chroma rounding bug in copy_image_to() yielding a controlled 58-byte overflow, the novel ASLR bypass that leaks libvips base addresses through uninitialized alpha-channel pixels in returned PNGs, the constrained write-what-where built from forged plane-map entries, and the clever reuse of libvips's internal g_module_open_full as a non-exported control-flow target eliminating the need for a ROP chain. Fix pollution at the boundary where untrusted bytes become objects, not in core

items.title: https://earendil.com/posts/prompt-caching/

ideas: Coding agent prompts mostly repeat prior turns, making prompt caching essential to agent economics

Same-meaning prompts that tokenize differently cannot share a KV cache
Session affinity keeps caches on one GPU; distributed KV blocks trade scheduling flexibility for systems complexity
Session trees mean one session ID maps to multiple prefixes with only partial cache overlap
Adding or reordering tools near the prompt start invalidates all cached conversation after the mismatch
Additive tool loading via deferred definitions extends tools mid-session without breaking the cached prefix
Extensions that rewrite prompts, shuffle tools, or inject timestamps can accidentally destroy entire-session caching
Anthropic's five-minute default cache TTL is shorter than many normal coding activities
Cache misses reprocess entire history at full input price, making trivial messages surprisingly expensive
Gateways billing uncached rates may profit from misses, so cache performance should be observable
Pruning old tool results rewrites prefixes and can cost more than future cache savings
Claude Code raises cache timeout to one hour for its own subscription users
items.rating_reason: This is dense, expert-level technical writing with multiple genuinely non-obvious insights: tool loadout changes invalidating cached conversation, additive tool loading via deferred definitions preserving prefixes, session trees creating partial-prefix cache fragmentation, and the counterintuitive finding that pruning history can cost more than it saves. items.title: M5Stack CoreS3 Tailscale: Direct UDP Drops WAV Download from 9s to 2.4s
items.summary: Porting Tailscale direct-UDP to ESP32-S3 surfaced an lwIP TCPIP-core reentrancy deadlock, an HTTP/2 WINDOW_CONTROL omission, and a DISCO probe-table exhaustion that together pinned traffic to DERP; fixing them quadrupled throughput.
ideas: lwIP's non-recursive TCPIP core lock deadlocks if WireGuard RX callback re-enters it
Tailscale DISCO Ping requires NaCl crypto_box, not XChaCha20-Poly1305
Constrained HTTP/2 clients must send WINDOW_UPDATE frames after receiving DATA
DISCO 64-entry probe table fills with unreachable peers, silently dropping new probes
Tailscale's home DERP selection picks lowest region ID, often a distant region
portable_terminal DISCO implementation already conformed to official packet formats

items.rating_reason: Exceptional first-hand debugging writeup documenting five distinct, non-obvious bugs encountered while porting Tailscale's networking stack to an ESP32-S3: a Tailscale DISCO protocol format mismatch, an lwIP double-locking deadlock inside the WireGuard RX callback, an HTTP/2 flow-control stall from missing WINDOW_UPDATE frames, a DISCO probe-table exhaustion caused by unreachable tailnet peers, and a DERP home-region selection bug picking the lowest region ID. Each finding is grounded in concrete logs, backtraces, code diffs, and 30-run before/after benchmarks (47 KiB/s → 187 KiB/s, 9 s → 2.4 s). Full game logic fits in one transformer layer within a 236-token context

It contains several genuinely non-obvious, reusable insights: the chessboard-parity argument that self-collisions only occur across even move gaps (halving required attention heads), length-conditioned inhibition of stale collision matches via negative weights, a deterministic food lookup table stored in position embeddings, and an additive unembedding trick that packs food and length into one token without combinatorial neurons. It is squarely relevant to LLM internals and interpretability interests, dense with concrete architecture details, and free of hype or padding. Minor limitations: it depends on part one of the series for some context, the game is admittedly a toy, and some passages are terse, but the mechanism-level knowledge delivered per minute is exceptional.

items.title: In Search of a Compositional Theory of Self-Stabilization
items.summary: Combining diagonal 'memory' entries with off-diagonal 'coupling' entries via eigenvalue analysis is necessary to correctly predict metastable failure in retry-storm systems, because small-gain reasoning alone ignores backlog carryover and gives falsely optimistic stability verdicts.
ideas: Parametric assume-guarantee contracts express behavior at every badness level, avoiding vacuous satisfaction outside the precondition.
Diagonal entries (11/12, 5/6) capture per-queue memory; off-diagonals (7/12, 1/6) capture cross-queue coupling.
Ignoring diagonal entries yields apparent loop gain 0.1; including them gives eigenvalue 1.19, predicting instability.
Retry budgets and fresh-first service both work by zeroing one coupling entry, restoring eigenvalues to 0.92 and 0.83.
Cap M=7 drains all starts; M≥8 introduces new attractors; M=40 parks system at (39,38) wasting 2/3 of capacity on duplicates.
Compositional self-stabilization theory has not advanced fundamentally since early 2000s, leaving metastable failures unaddressed.
Fixed point (8,4) balances arrivals with fresh service and retry rate with duplicate service.
items.rating_reason: Exceptional technical depth from a domain expert exploring compositional theory for self-stabilization. The article derives a concrete 4-entry Jacobian from the retry-storm model, computes eigenvalues (1.19 and 0.56), and explains mechanistically why known fixes (retry budgets, fresh-first service, capping) work by zeroing off-diagonal coupling entries. Honest about limitations—admits the parametric assume-guarantee formalism didn't fully apply due to its memoryless, single-scalar nature—but the analysis itself is original and rigorous. Highly relevant to distributed systems and resilience engineering.

items.summary: Agent harness quality determines how much model capability is wasted, and the highest-leverage decisions are instructive tool errors, content-hash read-before-edit, kernel-level path confinement, and pruning tool results before summarising.
ideas: Go 1.24 os.Root eliminates TOCTOU path races via kernel-level openat resolution
Read-before-edit should track per-path content hashes, not boolean read flags
POSIX forces SIGINT ignored in background children; use SIGTERM then SIGKILL
Prune stale tool-result bodies before spending a model call on summarisation
Estimate tokens via byte ratio corrected by EWMA over reported usage tokens
Tool error messages are implementation, not decoration, they are the model's recovery signal
Deny-only guard chains are monotonic, so ordering cannot weaken safety
Provider quirks belong in data profiles, not code branches
Never cut between assistant tool_calls and results; providers reject the whole request
Programmatic exit-code checks beat noisy LLM judges for eval harnesses
items.rating_reason: A dense, firsthand engineering write-up of a ~12k-line Go agent harness, packed with non-obvious mechanisms: content-hash read-before-edit versioning, Go 1.24 os.Root eliminating the TOCTOU path race at the kernel level, asymmetric truncation, monotonic deny-only guard chains, self-correcting token estimation, and the POSIX SIGINT-ignoring behavior of background shell children. It is directly relevant to LLM systems, agent tooling, and security, with honest caveats (bash not jailed, no time-to-first-token benefit from streaming) and no hype. Limitations: evidence is mostly qualitative design rationale rather than benchmarks, and the content truncates near the end, cutting the measurement section.

items.title: Ollama silently drops a history message larger than its context window
items.summary: Ollama drops whole history messages that exceed the model's trained context window, silently truncating without error, and the allocated window follows a simple min(requested, trained) rule.
ideas: Ollama allocates context size as min(requested, trained window) with no warning.
History messages larger than the window are removed entirely, not trimmed.
Compare prompt_eval_count with sent token count to detect dropped history.
Tokenizers differ widely; size context in tokens, not characters or bytes.
items.rating_reason: The article provides concrete, reproducible measurements of Ollama's context‑window handling, showing that oversized history messages are silently dropped and that the allocated window is clamped to the model's trained size. It includes token‑level data across multiple models and versions, a clear detection method (prompt_eval_count), and practical checks developers can use, making it highly relevant to AI/LLM engineering. While lengthy, the content stays focused on technical behavior without hype, though it assumes familiarity with Ollama APIs.

items.title: Installing HAProxy on OPNsense to replace Caddy

Maps assign hostnames to policies (e.g., INTERNAL_INFRA, EXTERNAL_DOCKERVM) for routing decisions.
ACME certificates are obtained via os‑acme‑client and reloaded automatically after renewal.
Disabling HTTP/2 in backend pools resolves long loading screens for Proxmox/TrueNAS interfaces.

It is highly relevant to sysadmin and infrastructure readers seeking practical reverse‑proxy migration details. Some introductory filler and GUI limitations add minor noise, preventing a perfect score.

items.title: https://darkmarc.substack.com/p/hijacking-ai-agents-how-an-agents
items.summary: Attackers can hijack AI agents by embedding malicious instructions in retrieved content, causing unauthorized actions.
ideas: AI agents treat fetched text as instructions, creating execution blind spots.
OWASP ranks Agent Goal Hijack as ASI01, the top agentic security risk.
Attackers embed malicious commands in web pages that agents retrieve.
Real attacks have used hijacked agents to steal crypto funds via bankr.
Compromised npm packages forced AI coding agents to exfiltrate secrets.
Calendar invites can hijack Gemini assistants, enabling unauthorized actions.
Cross‑browser agents share the same provenance flaw in instruction handling.
Input validation alone fails; all natural‑language inputs must be untrusted.
Indirect prompt injection can trigger transfers, data leaks, or system crashes.
Defense requires treating all fetched text as untrusted user input.
items.rating_reason: The piece uniquely defines Agent Goal Hijack as OWASP ASI01, explains how fetched text becomes executable instructions, and provides multiple concrete, documented exploits across crypto, npm, calendar invites, and cross‑browser agents, delivering extensive actionable insight. It dissects why traditional input validation fails and outlines clear mitigation principles. No significant padding or clickbait is present, avoiding major penalties.

items.title: https://www.securifera.com/blog/2026/09/21/one-login-two-rces-cve-2026-90822-and-cve-2026-90823/
items.summary: Combining protobuf misuse and unchecked strcpy creates a dual‑stage root exploit, but can be mitigated with proper input validation and hardened binaries.
ideas: Unchecked strcpy() into fixed buffer enables stack overflow ROP exploit
Protobuf fields concatenated into shell command cause OS command injection
XSS filter misses POSIX shell metacharacters, allowing command substitution
Multiple -g layers can write zero bytes via strcpy termination primitive
Shell expansion can compress payload to bypass command buffer size limits
Use of popen() without argument vector leads to unsafe command execution
Mitigation: replace unbounded copy with length check and remove shell from auth path
Rebuild native components with stack canaries, PIE, RELRO, fortified libc
items.rating_reason: The article delivers multiple concrete security insights, exploit techniques, and mitigation steps, providing high value for pentesters and defenders. It includes novel exploitation methods (protobuf‑to‑shell injection, multi‑layer strcpy trick) and practical remediation advice, with no clickbait or padding. Strong thematic relevance to CyberSecurity justifies a good score.

items.title: Audit your Agent files
items.summary: Regularly audit and prune agent configuration files to maintain efficiency and relevance.

Research shows 62% of repos have lint leakage and many exceed 200‑line limits.
Use Claude's /doctor command to audit unused skills, MCP servers, and context cost.
Personalized skills from individual history add little value versus generic community skills.
Keep context files focused on actionable project specifics, not generic advice.
Periodically audit and prune skills to avoid noise, token waste, and outdated rules.
Distinguish between installing a skill and retaining it; only keep high‑quality, well‑described skills.
Remember /doctor in sessions audits configuration, while shell claude doctor only shows diagnostics.
items.rating_reason: The article provides several concrete insights: it explains the half‑life of agent configuration files, cites research showing widespread bloat and lint leakage, demonstrates the practical use of Claude's /doctor command for auditing, and distinguishes between personalized and generic skills with empirical findings. It avoids fluff and clickbait, delivering high‑value, actionable guidance. No penalties apply, but the depth is strong yet not exceptional.

items.title: Brownfield Agentic Engineering
items.summary: Agents changed the price of attempting changes, not the evidence required to trust them—so gate autonomy to blast radius using zones, durable research artifacts, and pinned behavior.
ideas: Classify legacy code into green/yellow/red zones with autonomy levels matched to each zone's risk
A human must draw the zone map; agents left to choose start in the scariest files
Document only what code can't infer: trade-offs, conventions, history, unenforced guidelines
Capture agent research as cited comprehension memos since chat history is not a system of record
Plan and review with clean context rather than carrying the research session forward
Every repeated correction should be converted into a lint rule, test, hook, or skill
The harness becomes a durable record of failures the team decided not to pay for twice
Pin current behavior with characterization tests before letting agents change anything
Never let the same agent session author the tests it must pass
Half-finished migrations create contradictory precedent that badly confuses agents
A migration is complete only when the old path is demonstrably deleted, not ticketed
SWE Refactor Bench: only 28 of 520 agent runs passed the full migration audit
VB6-to-C# study showed 92% equivalence on simple features but 47% on complex ones—unit size is the lever
Write porting guides mapping old idioms to new before any agent runs (Bun's lesson)
Surface areas only production traffic understands are red zones until traffic stand-ins exist
Asana's $12k backlog clearance is a token bill, not a controlled savings study
Agents make attempting multiple rewrites cheap; human evaluation of trade-offs is unchanged

It backs claims with rare quantified evidence: SWE Refactor Bench's 28-of-520 migration audit pass rate, the VB6-to-C# 92%/47% equivalence study, Bun's 535k-line port, Stripe's 3.7M-line codemod, and Shopify's 12-week rewrite. Intellectual honesty is notable—caveats like Asana's $12k being a vendor-reported token bill, not a savings study. Minor conversational padding in the opening sections and an apparent mid-sentence truncation at the end prevent a higher score, but thematic relevance to AI-assisted engineering is exceptional.

items.title: An icosahedron on HDMI, drawn by a TxHDL core
items.summary: A full RISC-V SoC on an Artix-7 draws a rotating icosahedron on HDMI, illustrating how convexity eliminates the need for a depth buffer and how per-channel FIFOs cleanly cross clock domains between core and video peripheral.
ideas: Convexity removes depth buffer: positive z of unit normal tests visibility and lights.
Compose one row in a buffer, write each pixel once, eliminate clear-then-draw flicker.
Cross each AXI-Lite channel with its own FIFO since channels have no timing relationship.
Single brightness ramp of one tan, square-root spaced, plus 2x2 ordered dither quadruples perceived levels.
K-per-word serial protocol prevents UART buffer overrun when streaming programs.
65-entry quarter-wave sine table read forward/backward/negated covers full circle in fixed point.
Half-open fill rule with Q16 edge interpolation paints shared edges exactly once.
FPGA placement organically clusters subsystems near their I/O and adjacent logic.
items.rating_reason: Exceptional first-hand FPGA engineering writeup with concrete, non-obvious technical substance throughout: a RISC-V core written in a Rust-based HDL, clock-domain crossing per AXI-Lite channel via Gray-coded FIFOs, hidden-surface removal via convexity (z component doubles as visibility test and lighting intensity), single-pass row composition to avoid flicker without double buffering, and a K-acknowledged serial loader protocol. Every section contains reproducible detail (memory map, timings, code paths) with zero padding, hype, or career content.

items.title: Reversing the SH-4 fpu with the help of three AI models
items.summary: The SH‑4 FPU is a block of four truncated Booth multipliers, aligners, a four‑input adder and a single rounding stage, with FSCA/FSRRA implemented via small ROMs and feedback latches, all recovered through AI‑driven brute‑force analysis.
ideas: Four 24×24 truncated Booth multipliers feed a four‑input adder and one rounding stage.
FSCA and FSRRA use 17‑word and 34‑word coefficient ROMs with feedback latches.
AI models (Claude/Fable, GPT‑6 Astra, Opus) performed exhaustive searches on billions of input/output pairs.
Bit‑exact C implementation validates the reconstructed pipeline across millions of vectors.
Truncated design saves ~30 % area versus a fully IEEE‑rounded implementation.
items.rating_reason: The article provides a detailed, reproducible reverse‑engineering of the Dreamcast SH‑4 FPU, including concrete pipeline architecture, exhaustive test‑vector validation, and a publicly available bit‑exact C model. It demonstrates novel use of multiple AI models to explore a large hypothesis space, offering practical insights for emulators and low‑level hardware engineers. While the narrative is long, the technical depth and evidence outweigh the occasional anecdotal fluff, making it highly valuable to technically capable readers.

items.title: Scar of Quantization
items.summary: Outlier activations can leave irreversible quantization scars that stall validation loss, and fixing the scaling strategy (e.g., 1×32 or Hadamard rotation) can restore convergence.
ideas: Outlier activations can freeze a large fraction of a tile to zero during INT8 quantization, causing irreversible training scars.
Using 1×32 per‑token scaling instead of 1×32 per‑block reduces scar formation enough to enable convergence.
Hadamard rotation can spread outlier magnitude, improving signal‑to‑quantization‑noise ratio from 43.4 dB to 54.0 dB.
items.rating_reason: The article presents a clear, reproducible failure pattern in quantization aware training, showing how outlier activations create irreversible "scars" in INT8 tensors and quantifies their impact with concrete measurements (e.g., underflow rates, signal‑to‑quantization‑noise ratios). It offers a practical mitigation—switching to 1×32 scaling and experimenting with Hadamard rotation—to improve convergence, making the insight both technical and actionable for a specialist audience. The discussion is tightly focused on quantization mechanics rather than peripheral hype, though the evidence remains partly offline and not fully validated in a full training run.

items.title: Cache key injection: Smuggling poison through the door
items.summary: Manipulating cache key composition can let attackers poison shared caches, serve malicious content, and bypass security controls.

Attackers can bypass ACLs by splitting target paths across URI and header fragments.
Cache key collisions enable web cache deception without direct user interaction.

Manipulating scheme and host fragments can lead to stored XSS via cache poisoning.
The technique bypasses Cloudflare to poison Nginx origin caches.
Testing involves sending split requests to detect key collisions in black‑box environments.
Prevention requires bounded cache key construction and input sanitization.
items.rating_reason: The writeup delivers multiple novel, actionable insights—cache key collision attacks via fragment manipulation, cache deception bypassing ACLs, CPDoS via key collisions, and HTTP scheme injection for stored XSS—clearly explained with practical Nginx and Cloudflare examples. items.title: Seeing through the template black magic
items.summary: Empirical test shows GCC 16 and Clang 22 generate essentially identical machine code from plain C functions with constant arguments as from Boost's deep C++ template tower, when the function body is visible at the call site.
ideas: Modern compilers fold constants from plain C functions as effectively as from C++ template specializations

Merging multiple template instances into one function is the optimizer's work, not the templates'

items.title: What actually is a Docker container?
items.summary: Linux containers are not lightweight VMs: isolation is implemented per-process via namespace pointers in task_struct, so the same kernel answers the same syscalls differently depending on the calling process's nsproxy.
ideas: Containers share the host kernel; isolation happens at syscall-resolution time via per-process namespace pointers, not virtualization.
UID 0 inside a user namespace only holds capabilities relative to that namespace, not the initial one.
The kernel checks ns_capable on the user_ns that owns the target resource (e.g., uts_ns->user_ns for sethostname).
/proc/self/ns entries expose the namespace instance a process belongs to via inode numbers.
user_ns lives in cred, not nsproxy, because it is credential state rather than a per-namespace resource.
Mac/Windows Docker runtimes need a Linux VM because macOS/Windows kernels lack the required namespace and cgroup features.
items.rating_reason: Exceptionally mechanism-focused explainer that walks through Linux kernel source (task_struct, nsproxy, kernel/sys.c) to show exactly how containers differ from VMs and how namespace isolation is implemented per-process rather than via virtualization. Uses a reproducible test program and references real CVEs (CVE-2022-0185, CVE-2024-1086), capabilities, and UID mapping to demonstrate non-obvious behaviors like 'root inside' not being 'root outside'. Truncation at the PID namespace section is a meaningful limitation, and some territory is familiar to seasoned kernel engineers, but the kernel-source-grounded explanation is genuinely instructive.

Fix with tojson(sort_keys=True) in the chat template or sort schema keys in the gateway
Measure prompt_tokens_cached_total/prompt_tokens_total, not GPU hit counters, to gauge cache health

Speculative decoding looks bad at low cache hit rates but wins once the cache is warm
Place stable prompt content first; volatile per-agent and live status text last
Report cache hit rate alongside any LLM latency benchmark

It also documents non-obvious hybrid-attention cache behavior (2048-token block boundaries that make CPU KV offload nearly useless) and a practical, evidence-backed checklist including the finding that speculative decoding's verdict flips once the cache is warm. Relevance to the reader's LLM-systems and agent-engineering interests is direct, and the density of measurements, configs, and reproducible debugging steps is very high. items.title: Fragnesia primitive via Open vSwitch. Deterministic local privilege escalation.
items.summary: Open vSwitch unintentionally clears the shared‑frag flag during failed upcalls, re‑enabling the Fragnesia in‑place decryption primitive for root escalation.
ideas: Open vSwitch strips SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG during failed userspace upcalls, re‑exposing Fragnesia bug.
The bug lets unprivileged users trigger in‑place ESP decryption on read‑only pages.
Exploit works on default installs of major distros with user namespaces enabled.
It exploits zero‑copy flag interactions and MSG_ZEROCOPY with DONT_ORPHAN.
skb_tx_error() clears the shared‑frag marker, breaking the ownership invariant.
Attack requires building a datapath and installing a flow with USERSPACE then OUTPUT actions.
Kernel fixes propagated shared‑frag marker through many helpers but missed the OVS path.
The issue is tracked as CVE‑2026‑90049, CVE‑2026‑89487, and CVE‑2026‑80977.
Verification uses a kprobe on skb_tx_error() showing the flag cleared after the call.
Exploit writes attacker‑chosen bytes into a root‑owned file's page cache via ESP decryption.
